slides.title: Same résumé, different name: who gets called back?
slides.sub: A walk-through of the field experiment by [c|Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004)], with every number recomputed from the public replication data.
slides.say: Two résumés, identical in every line except the name at the top. The question is whether that one line changes who gets a call.

slides.title: The experiment sent {n} fictitious résumés to real job ads and changed only the name

steps.t: Write résumés of higher and lower quality, modelled on real applicants.
Give each résumé a [a|White-sounding] or an [b|African-American-sounding] name at random.
Send them in reply to help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago.
Record whether the employer calls back to offer an interview.

note.t: Because the name was assigned at random, a difference in callbacks can be attributed to the name itself and not to the applicant's record.

slides.say: Walk through the four steps slowly. The point to land is the last line: random assignment is what lets us read the gap as the effect of the name.

slides.title: [a|White-sounding names] drew {ratio} more callbacks than [b|African-American-sounding names]
notes: Employers called back {rate_white} of the résumés with White-sounding names and {rate_black} of those with African-American-sounding names.

notes.t: Put differently, one callback took about {per_callback_white} résumés under a White-sounding name and about {per_callback_black} under an African-American-sounding one.

slides.caption: Share of résumés that received a callback, with {ci_level} Wilson intervals; {n_group} résumés in each group. The test is a two-sided test of proportions.
slides.say: Show the two bars first and let the room read them. Then the difference, then the test. Do not rush to the stars.

slides.title: Better résumés seemed to help [a|White-sounding names] more, but the gap is too imprecise to confirm
notes: Higher quality added {quality_gain_white} percentage points for White-sounding names.

notes.t: For African-American-sounding names it added only {quality_gain_black} points.
The difference between these two returns is {m3_blackxhigh_b} points with a standard error of {m3_blackxhigh_se}, so equal returns cannot be ruled out.

slides.caption: Callback rate by résumé quality, with {ci_level} Wilson intervals.
slides.say: Be careful here. The direction is suggestive, but say plainly that the interaction is imprecise and that equal returns cannot be ruled out.

slides.title: The penalty for an [b|African-American-sounding name] is negative and significant in all four models

chart.axis: Change in callback probability, percentage points

slides.caption: Linear probability models of a callback; coefficients in percentage points, robust standard errors in parentheses. The plot shows the last model with {ci_level} intervals. Controls are sex, city and years of experience.
slides.say: Start with the first row only. Then bring in the other coefficients and point out that the penalty barely moves across the columns.

slides.title: The gap appears in both cities: {gap_boston} points in Boston and {gap_chicago} in Chicago

figure.source: Figure 2 of the specimen paper (stand-in drawn by make_paper_figure.py)

notes: The published figure reports callback rates for all résumés and separately by city.

notes.t: In Boston the rates are {rate_white_boston} and {rate_black_boston}; in Chicago they are {rate_white_chicago} and {rate_black_chicago}.

slides.caption: Top row of the original figure, shown unaltered; the panel on résumé quality is left out here.
slides.say: This is the figure as published. Zoom into the city panel and read the two pairs of bars aloud.

slides.title: A name alone changed who was called back, and a stronger résumé did not clearly close the gap
points: Identical résumés drew {ratio} more callbacks under a [a|White-sounding name] than under an [b|African-American-sounding name].
The penalty remains negative and statistically significant after controlling for résumé quality, sex, city and experience.
Whether better qualifications pay off less under an African-American-sounding name remains open in these data.
slides.refs: [c|Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? American Economic Review, 94(4), 991–1013. Data: ResumeNames in the R package AER.]
slides.say: Three sentences, in this order. End on the open question, and point to the code for anyone who wants the paper.
